case_study_insert.main_stem: Tidewater Surfwear (TSW) is a private limited company in the coastal apparel retail sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2016 by Elena Marlow, the business sells surfwear through its website and a small chain of seaside stores, and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. TSW plans to invest $540,000 in a new automated fabric-cutting and printing facility, financed by a $300,000 bank loan and a $240,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $162,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $39.00, and currently produces 15,000 units a year. TSW faces two problems: fabric waste has reached 11% of material use and delivery complaints are rising as online orders grow.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — Q3 2025: The cutting room produced 3,750 garments last quarter with a fabric-waste rate of 11%, down from 15% a year ago. End-of-line quality control inspection found a 2.6% defect rate, improved from 4.1%. Customer complaints fell from 52 to 30 per month. Average online order dispatch time is 3.4 days. A survey of 500 buyers found 61% rank fit and comfort as the top purchase factor, and 44% would pay 8% more for ethically made surfwear. A quality assurance review recommends preventing waste by training cutting operators, at $600 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Tidewater Surfwear as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank lifted the base rate from 4.0% to 4.75%, raising interest on TSW's $300,000 bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage will increase 6.0% to $13.25 an hour from April 2026, affecting TSW's workforce of 40. (3) Wholesale cotton and synthetic fabric costs rose 11.3% year-on-year, while consumer spending on apparel grew 2.1% and the sector's average online return rate is 18%.

questions.question_text: TSW plans to finance part of its $540,000 cutting-facility investment with a $240,000 share issue rather than a larger bank loan. Explain two advantages for TSW of using this share issue.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A $240,000 share issue brings in equity that needs no interest payments or capital repayment, so it protects TSW's cash flow while the business already meets fixed costs of $162,000 a year and loses material to an 11% fabric-waste rate. Unlike the $300,000 bank loan, the share money does not add to interest charges if the base rate rises, leaving more of the $39.00 selling price to cover the 11.3% rise in fabric input costs and keeping cash available for the $540,000 facility.

Point 2: Because the $240,000 is equity rather than debt, no lender can repossess the new $540,000 facility if demand for surfwear disappoints, reducing financial risk for a 40-employee coastal retailer dependent on seasonal trade. The $240,000 also enlarges the shareholder base, bringing fresh capital and potentially new contacts or retail experience, which can support Elena Marlow's plans to grow the seaside stores and website alongside the automated cutting line.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to TSW's costs, waste, financing mix and expansion.

questions.question_text: TSW wants to grow sales of its surfwear range. Consider selling only through its own website, listing on a large third-party online marketplace, or expanding its independent seaside stores. Which should TSW choose as its main growth channel? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Own website only: Selling direct through its own website keeps all the $39.00 selling price and builds first-party customer data, which helps TSW target the 44% of surveyed buyers who would pay 8% more for ethically made surfwear. It avoids marketplace commission. However, a small brand with a workforce of 40 will struggle to attract traffic without heavy promotion, and the website alone cannot deliver the volume needed to justify the $540,000 automated cutting facility.

Third-party online marketplace: A large marketplace gives instant access to millions of shoppers and low setup cost, filling the new facility's capacity quickly and supporting the 15,000-unit output. The drawbacks are commission on each sale and intense price competition that would undercut the 8% ethical premium, plus no direct customer list and less control over how TSW's surfwear is presented, which may conflict with its sustainability positioning.

Independent seaside stores: Physical stores let customers feel fit and comfort, which the survey shows matters to 61% of buyers, and they build local brand loyalty in TSW's coastal heartland. Yet stores carry high fixed costs, which would add to the $162,000 already incurred, and reach far fewer customers than online channels, so they cannot be the main growth engine.

Recommendation: TSW should choose its own website as the main growth channel, using stores as showrooms and a limited marketplace listing only for clearance. Direct online sales protect margin and customer data, unlike the marketplace, and scale nationally unlike stores, so they best utilise the $540,000 facility. Stores are rejected as too costly and slow to grow; the marketplace is rejected because commission and price competition destroy the ethical premium TSW is trying to build.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the channels with minimal application to TSW.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two channels in the context of TSW with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three channels in the context of TSW with a well-justified recommendation explaining why stores and marketplace are rejected.

questions.question_text: TSW's fabric waste has reached 11% and its hierarchical structure is led autocratically by Elena Marlow. Explain two benefits for TSW of this structure and leadership style when tackling the waste problem.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A hierarchical structure with a clear chain of command lets Elena Marlow set firm waste-reduction targets quickly and communicate them down through supervisors to the cutting room, which suits an urgent 11% fabric-waste rate. Decisions are not delayed by consultation, so TSW can respond faster than a flat structure when the 15% waste figure of a year ago is being improved upon, protecting the $39.00 selling price from wasted material.

Point 2: Autocratic leadership gives decisive control over the introduction of the new $540,000 automated cutting facility, with tight standards on how operators use fabric. Clear roles and close supervision reduce the 2.6% defect rate further and help bring delivery complaints down from 52 to 30 per month, because supervisors can enforce consistent cutting routines across the workforce of 40 without waiting for group agreement. This fast, top-down response matters because the 11% waste rate adds cost to every one of the 15,000 units produced.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual analysis linked to TSW's waste, defect rate, complaints and structure.

questions.question_text: TSW wants to reduce its 2.6% defect rate and 11% fabric waste. Consider end-of-line quality control inspection or a quality assurance approach that prevents faults through training. Which should TSW choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Quality control inspection: Checking finished garments at the end of the line catches defects before they reach customers, which addresses the 2.6% defect rate directly and protects TSW's reputation with the 61% of buyers who rank fit and comfort highly. It is simple to operate within the hierarchical structure. However, inspection happens after material has already been wasted, so it does little to cut the 11% fabric-waste rate, and rejected garments add rework cost that squeezes the $27.00 contribution per unit.

Quality assurance through training: Preventing faults by training cutting operators at $600 per employee tackles the source of both the 2.6% defects and the 11% waste, and the quality assurance review in Appendix 1 recommends exactly this. With 40 staff, full training would cost $24,000, affordable against the $540,000 investment. The drawback is that results are slower to appear, training takes operators away from the line, and a prevention culture is harder to enforce under autocratic leadership without genuine staff involvement.

Decision: TSW should choose quality assurance through training as its main approach, retaining a light final inspection as a safety net. Prevention attacks the 11% waste that inspection cannot fix and reduces rework on every unit, protecting the $39.00 price. Pure inspection is rejected because it only detects faults after costly material is wasted; doing nothing is rejected because the 2.6% defect rate and 52 monthly complaints show the current approach is not enough. TSW should review the defect rate monthly against the 4.1% figure of a year ago to confirm the training is working.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of quality control and quality assurance with limited application to TSW.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both approaches in the context of TSW.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both approaches with a well-justified decision covering waste, cost and leadership fit.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how TSW's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $162,000 ÷ ($39.00 − $12.00) = $162,000 ÷ $27.00 = 6,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 6,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $39.00 − $12.00 = $27.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $27.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways TSW's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 6,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 15,000 units to confirm the surfwear range is profitable, leaving a margin of safety of 9,000 units, which supports going ahead with the $540,000 cutting facility.
2. Use average total cost of $162,000 ÷ 15,000 units + $12.00 = $22.80 a unit to monitor the effect of the 11% fabric waste, setting a target to bring unit cost down toward the $12.00 variable cost as waste falls.
3. Use contribution per unit of $27.00 to judge whether the 8% ethical premium sought by 44% of surveyed buyers is worth pursuing, since even a small price rise adds directly to contribution on 15,000 units.
4. Use labour productivity of 15,000 units ÷ 40 staff = 375 units per worker to benchmark the automated cutting line, linking the 2.6% defect rate and falling complaints to output per employee before adding capacity.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 6,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $27.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 15,000-unit output; average total cost of $22.80 to track 11% waste; contribution analysis of the 8% ethical premium; and labour productivity of 375 units per worker.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TSW's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has TSW's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.64 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.78 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.57 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.81 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $150,000 inventories + $55,000 trade receivables + $25,000 cash = $230,000; 2025 current assets = $130,000 + $70,000 + $40,000 = $240,000. The 2024 figure is $230,000 ÷ $140,000 = 1.64; the 2025 figure is $240,000 ÷ $135,000 = 1.78. Excluding stock, 2024 liquid assets are $55,000 + $25,000 = $80,000, giving $80,000 ÷ $140,000 = 0.57; 2025 liquid assets are $70,000 + $40,000 = $110,000, giving $110,000 ÷ $135,000 = 0.81.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved on both measures. The 1.64 to 1.78 rise shows current assets cover short-term debts more comfortably, helped by current liabilities falling from $140,000 to $135,000 while cash doubled from $25,000 to $40,000. The 0.57 to 0.81 improvement is especially welcome because it shows TSW is less reliant on selling stock to pay debts, important while it services a $300,000 loan and invests $540,000 in new capacity. Nevertheless, trade receivables rose from $55,000 to $70,000, tying up cash, and the stock-excluding measure at 0.81 still means liquid assets do not fully cover liabilities, so a sudden fall in demand could expose the business.

Conclusion: TSW's financial position has improved. Both measures rose and the improvement is not just an inventory effect, since inventories actually fell from $150,000 to $130,000. The main residual risk is higher receivables, so TSW should tighten credit control while proceeding with the cutting facility.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether TSW's position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TSW of sourcing ethically made surfwear as promoted in its market research.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Ethically made surfwear matches the 44% of 500 surveyed buyers who would pay 8% more, so TSW can lift its $39.00 selling price and add directly to the $27.00 contribution per unit, helping to justify the $540,000 cutting-facility investment. It also strengthens the brand with the 61% who put fit and comfort first by associating the product with quality and responsibility, which supports repeat purchases and fewer complaints in the seaside stores.

Disadvantage: Ethical and certified fabrics usually cost more than standard material, raising the $12.00 variable cost per unit and squeezing contribution unless the full 8% premium is accepted by customers. The insert does not quantify the extra fabric cost, so the effect can only be judged qualitatively; if the premium is not won, TSW's 2.6% defect rate and 11% fabric waste will be even harder to absorb, and the 8% claim could be criticised as unsupported marketing.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to TSW's survey, costs and waste.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise from 4.0% to 4.75%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in fabric input costs will affect TSW. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): If TSW's $300,000 loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $300,000 = $2,250 a year (0.0075 × $300,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $162,000 a year, and if the loan is fixed the effect is zero. Higher rates could dampen consumer spending on apparel, which grew only 2.1%, and make future borrowing for the $540,000 facility dearer, but TSW can reduce this risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $13.25 per hour): With a workforce of 40, this rise feeds into TSW's wage bill and cannot be avoided in cutting, printing and store roles. The insert does not state hours worked or each worker's pay, so no defensible annual total can be invented. The correct test is the given productivity figure: 15,000 units ÷ 40 staff = 375 units per worker. If productivity holds at 375 units or output rises, the wage rise is affordable; otherwise unit labour cost climbs and the $27.00 contribution per unit falls.

Fabric input cost inflation (11.3%): The insert does not break down the $12.00 variable cost, so only a bound can be calculated: if the whole variable cost rose 11.3%, that adds 11.3% × $12.00 = about $1.36 per unit, or roughly $20,400 a year at 15,000 units. Even a smaller increase in cotton and synthetics would erode contribution, and with apparel spending up only 2.1% and the sector return rate at 18%, TSW may struggle to pass the cost on through its $39.00 price.

Conclusion: The 11.3% rise in fabric input costs will have the greatest impact. It hits every unit produced, directly threatening the $27.00 contribution that supports the $540,000 expansion, and it compounds with the existing 11% fabric waste. The interest rise costs only about $2,250 and the wage rise can be offset if 375-unit productivity holds, so fabric inflation is the larger threat.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to TSW.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on TSW's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of TSW with a well-justified judgment on which has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
